readings.c1s1:
¶
'''wool-work''' (wu̇l′wėrk), ''n.'' Needlework imitating tapestry, usually done on canvas with Berlin wools. The name is sometimes given to other forms of embroidery with wools.—'''Mosaic wool-work.''' {{smaller|See ''mosaic''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''woom''' (wöm), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] A trade-name for the fur of the beaver. There are four sorts—silvery, pale, white, and brown.

'''woon<sup>1</sup>''' (wön), ''n.'' [< Burmese ''wun'', a burden.] An administrative officer; a governor: as, myo-''woon'', chief governor; ye-''woon'', water-governor; ''woon''-gyre, high minister, or member of the council of state.
{{smaller block|The most arbitrary confiscation of their goods by every petty ''Woon'' who flourished one gold umbrella.
{{right|''J. W. Palmer'', Up and Down the Irrawaddi, p. 36.}}}}

'''woon<sup>2</sup>†.''' A variant of ''wone''<sup>2</sup>, ''won''<sup>2</sup>, ''won''<sup>4</sup>.

'''woont†''', ''v.'' An obsolete form of ''wont''<sup>1</sup>. ''Spenser.''

'''woorali, woorara, woorari''' (wö′ra-li, -rä, -ri), ''n.'' South American arrow-poison: same as ''curari''. Also ''wourali'', ''wourari''.
{{smaller block|Upon the application of a stimulus . . . contractions will still take place after the animal has been poisoned by ''woorara'', which is known to paralyze the motor set of nerves. {{right|''J. M. Carnochan'', Operative Surgery, p. 116.}}}}

'''woorst†''', ''a.'' An obsolete form of ''worst''.

'''woose†''', ''n.'' An earlier form of ''ooze''.
{{smaller block|The aguish ''woose'' of Kent and Essex.
{{right|''Howell'', Vindication, 1677 (Harl. Misc., VI. 129).}}}}

'''woost†.''' A variant of ''wost'', second person singular indicative present of ''wit''<sup>1</sup>.

'''woosy†''', ''a.'' An earlier form of ''oozy''.
{{smaller block|What is she else, but a foul ''woosy'' Marsh?
{{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, xxv. 205.}}}}
readings.c1s2:
¶
'''woot†.''' A Middle English form of ''wot''. See ''wit''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''

'''wootz''' (wöts), ''n.'' [Supposed to be an orig. error or misprint, perhaps for *''wook'', repr. Canarese ''ukku'' (pron. wukku), steel.] The name given to steel made in India by fusing iron with carbonaceous matter. {{smaller|This is done in small crucibles holding a pound or two of the iron, and the wood selected to furnish the carbon to the metal is always that of ''Cassia auriculata'', which is cut into small pieces, the same being done with the iron, and the whole covered by one or more green leaves, usually of a species of ''Convolvulus'', the crucible being then covered with a lid of clay. A number of these crucibles are placed together in a hole dug in the ground, and heated in a charcoal-fire urged by a pair of bellows made of ox-hide, the blast being kept up for three or four hours. The steel thus obtained is hard in temper, and requires much care in working. This is the oldest method of making steel of which anything definite is known, having been in use, without change, for an indefinite length of time, and being, as generally believed, original with the Hindus.}}

'''wop''' (wop), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''wopped'', ppr. ''wopping''. Same as ''whop''.
{{smaller block|Old Osborne was highly delighted when Georgy ''wopped'' her third boy . . . in Russell Square.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Vanity Fair, lvi.}}}}

'''wopen†.''' An obsolete strong past participle of ''weep''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wops''' (wops), ''n.'' [A variant of ''waps'' for ''wasp''.] A wasp or hornet. Also ''wopps''. [Prov. Eng.]

'''worble''' (wôr′bl), ''n.'' Same as ''wabble''<sup>2</sup> or ''warble''<sup>3</sup>, 3.

Canarese ''ukku'' (pron. wukku), steel.]   The name given to steel made in India by fusing iron with carbonaceous matter. {{smaller|This is done in small crucibles holding a pound or two of the iron, and the wood selected to furnish the carbon to the metal is always that of ''Cassia auriculata'', which is cut into small pieces, the same being done with the iron, and the whole covered by one or more green leaves, usually of a species of ''Convolvulus'', the crucible being then covered with a lid of clay. '''Worcester porcelain.''' See ''porcelain''<sup>1</sup>.

'''word'''<sup>1</sup> (wėrd), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''woord;'' < ME. ''word'', ''wurd'', ''weord'' (pl. ''word'', ''wordes''), < AS. ''word'' (pl. ''word'') = OS. ''word'' = OFries. ''word'', ''werd'', ''wird'' = D. LG. ''woord'' = OHG. MHG. G. ''wort'' = Icel. ''orth'' (for *''vord'') = Sw. Dan. ''ord'' = Goth. ''waurd'', a word, = Lith. ''wardas'', a name, = L. ''verbum'', a word, verb; orig. ‘a thing spoken’; cf. Gr. εἴρειν, speak, ἐρεῖν, question, ῥήτωρ, speaker, etc. (see ''rhetor''). Doublet of ''verb''.]   '''1.''' A sound, or combination of sounds, used in any language as the sign of a conception, or of a conception together with its grammatical relations; the smallest bit of human language forming a grammatical part of speech; a vocable; a term. {{smaller|A word may be any part of speech, as verb, noun, particle, etc.; it may be radical, as ''love'', or derivative, as ''lover'', ''lovely'', ''loveliness'', or an inflected form, as ''loves'', ''loved;'' it may be simple, or compound, as ''love-sick''. Anything is a word that can be used as an individual member of a sentence, and that is not separable into parts usable independently and coördinately in making a sentence. A word is a spoken sign that has arrived at its value as used in any language by a series of historical changes, and that holds its value by virtue of usage, being exposed to such further changes, of form and of meaning, as usage may prescribe. The conception involved in a word may be of any grade, from the simplest, as ''one'', to the most derived and complicated, as ''political'', and the grammatical relations involved may also be of any degree, from ''true'' to ''untruthfulness'', or from (Latin) ''ama'' to ''amabitur''.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Geffray the letters after breke and rayd,
Fro ''wurde'' unto ''wurd''.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3187.}}}}
{{smaller block|Sixe ''wordes'' out of which all the whole dittie is made, euery of those sixe commencing and ending his verse by course.
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 72.}}}}
438

{{smaller block|''Words'' are but the current tokens or marks of popular notions of things.
{{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii.215.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Words'' are sensible signs necessary for communication.
{{right|''Locke'', Human Understanding, III. ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The deeper and more complex parts of human nature can be exhibited by means of ''words'' alone.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Moore’s Byron.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Words'', which are a set of clickings, hissings, lispings, and so on, mean very little, compared to tones and expression of the features.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, viii.}}}}
'''2.''' The letter or letters or other characters, written or printed, which represent such a vocable: as, a ''word'' misprinted.—'''3.''' Speech; talk; discourse; conversation: commonly in the plural.
{{smaller block|Whan Melior that meke mayde herd Alisaundrines ''wordes'', sche was gretly gladed of hire gode bi-hest.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 600.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I would not, in plain terms, from this time forth,
Have you so slander any moment’s leisure
As to give ''words'' or talk with the Lord Hamlet.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 3. 134.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Men began to murmur against Captain Swan for perswading them to come this Voyage; but he gave them fair ''words''.
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 282.}}}}
{{smaller block|Can there be no sympathy without the gabble of ''words?''
{{right|''Lamb'', Quakers’ Meeting.}}}}
'''4.''' Saying; remark; expression: as, a ''word'' of comfort or sympathy; a ''word'' of reproach.
{{smaller block|<poem>Him wil I cheare with chaunting al this night;
And with that ''word'' she gan to cleare hir throate.</poem>
{{right|''Gascoigne'', Philomene (ed. Arber), p. 88.}}}}
'''5.''' A symbol of thought, as distinguished from thought itself; sound as opposed to sense.

{{smaller block|The majority attend to ''words'' rather than to things.
{{right|''Descartes'', Prin. of Philos. (tr. by Veitch), i. § 74.}}}}
{{smaller block|Life is short, and conversation apt to run to mere ''words''.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|To modern society Antinomians and Socinians are but ''words'', are but ancient history.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXLIII. 23.}}}}
'''6.''' Intelligence; information; tidings; report: without an article, and used only as a singular: as, to send ''word'' of one’s arrival.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ye noblist of nome that neuer man adouted,
The ''worde'' of your wekes & your wight dedis,
And the prise of your prowes passes o fer!</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S), l. 1098.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll send him certain ''word'' of my success.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 4. 89.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Word'' is to the kitchen gane,
And ''word'' is to the ha’,
And ''word'' is to the noble room,
Amang the ladyes a’.</poem>
{{right|''The Queen’s Marie'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 116).}}}}
{{smaller block|I did give them an account dismayed them all, and ''word'' was carried in to the King.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, II. 440.}}}}
'''7.''' An expression of will or decision; an injunction; command; order.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sharp ’s the ''word;'' egad, I’ll own the thing.</poem>
{{right|''Vanburgh'', The Mistake, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|In my time a father’s ''word'' was law.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Dora.}}}}
'''8.''' A password; a watchword; a war-cry; a signal, or term of recognition, even when consisting of several words.
{{smaller block|<poem>Advance our standards, set upon our foes;
Our ancient ''word'' of courage, fair Saint George,
Inspire us with the spleen of fiery dragons!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., v. 3. 349.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I have the ''word;'' sentonel, do thou stand;
Thou shalt not need to call, I’ll be at hand.</poem> {{right|''Fletcher and Rowley'', Maid in the Mill, iv. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Let the ''word'' be: Not without mustard; your crest is very rare, sir.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, iii. 1.}}}}
'''9†.''' A brief or pithy remark or saying; a proverb; a motto.
{{smaller block|The old ''word'' is “What the eye views not, the heart rues not.” {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Balm of Gilead, xi. § 5.}}}}
'''10.''' Affirmation; promise; obligation; good faith; a term or phrase implying or containing an assertion, declaration, assurance, or the like, which involves the faith or honor of the utterer of it: with a possessive: as, I pledge you ''my word;'' on ''my word'', sir.
{{smaller block|They are not men o’ ''their words''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 6. 106.}}}}
{{smaller block|Madam, I dare pass ''my word'' for her truth.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Doll.'' Alas, Master Allum, ’t is but poor fifty pound!
''All.'' If that be all, you shall upon ''your word'' take up so much with me; another time I’ll run as far in your books. {{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Old as I am, I take thee at ''thy word.''
{{right|''Dryden'', Conquest of Granada, II., ii. i.}}}}
{{smaller block|I hope you’l think it no way improper, and must beg of you it may be done, because ''my word'’s at stake.
{{right|''E. Gibson'', in Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 230.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Our'' royal ''word'' upon it,
He comes back safe. ''Tennyson'', Princess, v.</poem>}}
'''11.''' Utterances or terms interchanged expressive of anger, contention, or reproach: in the plural, and often qualified by ''high'', ''hot'', ''hard'', ''sharp'', or the like.

{{smaller block|Some ''words'' there grew ’twixt Somerset and me.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., ii. 5. 46.}}}}
{{smaller block|She and I had some ''words'' last Sunday at church, but I think I gave her her own. ''Swift'', Polite Conversation, i.
Having had some ''words'' with Bemoy, he stabbed him with his dagger to the heart, so that he fell dead without uttering a word. ''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, II. 102.
<poem>He and I
Had once ''hard words'', and parted.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Dora.</poem>}}}}
'''12.''' In ''theol.'': (''a'') [''cap.''] The Son of God; God as manifested to man: same as ''Logos.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou, my ''Word'', begotten Son, by thee
This I perform. ''Milton'', P. L., vii. 163.</poem>}}
(''b'') [''cap.'' or ''l. c.''] The Holy Scripture, or a part of Scripture: as, the ''Word'' of God, or God’s ''Word.''
{{smaller block|The excellency of this ''Word'' is so great, and of so high dignity, that there is no earthly thing to be compared unto it. ''Latimer'', 1st Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1549.
For, when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the ''Word'', by and by he is offended. Mat. xiii. 21.
Deliuered in Six Sermons at Steeple-Ashton in Wiltshire by George Webbe, Preacher of the ''Word'' and Pastor there. ''The Practice of Quietness'' (1615).
The sword and the ''word!'' do you study them both, master parson? ''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 1. 44.
You say there must be no Human Invention in the Church, nothing but the pure ''word.''
{{right|''Selden'', Table-Talk, p. 58.}}}}
{{smaller|'''A play upon words.''' See ''play''<sup>1</sup>.—'''At short words†.''' See ''short.''—'''A word and a blow,''' a threat and its immediate execution; hastiness in action: also used adjectively.}}
{{smaller block|I find there is nothing but ''a word and a blow'' with you.
{{right|''Swift'', Polite Conversation, i. (''Davies.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|A Napoleon-like promptitude of action, which the unlearned operatives described by calling him “''a word-and-a-blow'' man.” {{right|''Mrs. Trollope'', Michael Armstrong, iv. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''By word of mouth.''' See ''mouth.''

{{smaller block|Howbeit, this matter may be easily remedied, if you will take the pains to ask the question of Raphael himself, ''by word of mouth'', if he be now with you.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia, Ded. to Peter Giles, p. 8.}}}}

{{smaller block|“This,” he said, “is not a court in which written charges are exhibited. Our proceedings are summary, and ''by word of mouth.''” {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}}

'''Fallacy in words.''' See ''semiological fallacy'', under ''fallacy.'' —'''God’s Word.''' Same as ''the Word of God'', below.—'''Good word''', favorable account or mention; expression of good opinion; commendation; praise: as, to speak a ''good word'' for one.
{{smaller block|<poem>Where your ''good word'' cannot advantage him,
Your slander never can endamage him.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 2. 42.}}}}

'''Hard words.''' (''a'') Words not easy to spell, pronounce, or define correctly. (''b'') Hot, angry, or reproachful words. See def. 11, and the quotation there from Tennyson.—'''Homophonous words.''' See ''homophonous.''—'''Household word.''' See ''household.''—'''In a word, in one word''', in one brief, pithy phrase; briefly; to sum up; in short.
{{smaller block|<poem>''In a word'', for far behind his worth
Comes all the praises that I now bestow,
He is complete in feature and in mind.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 4. 71.}}}}

{{smaller block|''In a word'', to be a fine gentleman is to be a generous and a brave man. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 75.}}}}

{{smaller block|Here, ''in a word''—and it is a rare instance in my life—I had met with a person thoroughly adapted to the situation which he held. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 27.}}}}

'''In word''', in speech only; hence, in mere profession or seeming.

{{smaller block|Let us not love ''in word'', neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth. {{right|1 John iii. 18.}}}} '''Mind the word.''' See ''mind''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Precatory words.''' See ''precatory''.—'''The Comfortable Words.''' See ''comfortable''.—'''The Word of God,''' the Bible; the Scriptures. This use is rejected by the Society of Friends, who limit the phrase to the meaning given in def. 12 (''a'').

{{smaller block|An account of a personal pressure brought to bear upon Fisher by the King, who pointed out to him that his obedience was limited by the condition “so far as ''the Word of God'' allowed.” {{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XXVI. 885.}}}}
'''To be as good as one’s word.''' See ''good''.—'''To break one’s word, to break word†.''' See ''break''.—'''To eat one’s words.''' See ''eat''.—'''To have a word''' with a person, to have some conversation with him.
{{smaller block|<poem>The friar and you
Must ''have a word'' anon.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1. 364.}}}}
'''To have the words for†,''' to act as spokesman for.
{{smaller block|<poem>Our hoste ''hadde the wordes for'' us alle.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Parson’s Tale, l. 67.}}}}
'''To make words.''' See ''make''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To pass one’s word.''' See ''pass''.—'''Word and end†,''' from beginning to end; everything.
{{smaller block|<poem>Of al this werk he tolde hym ''worde and ende.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 702.}}}}
'''Word for word,''' in the exact words or terms; verbatim; literally.
{{smaller block|And he wrote in hys booke ''worde for worde'' like as he hym tolde. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 259.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Court.'' Do you read on then.——
''Free.'' [Reads.] . . .
''Court.'' ''Word for word.''</poem>
{{right|''Etherege'', She Would if She Could, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|I shall set it [a letter] down ''word for word'' as it came to me. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Who with the News to Procris quick repair’d,
Repeating ''Word for Word'' what she had heard.</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', tr. of Ovid’s Art of Love.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
